title: Smartphone-Based Screening Colorimetry for APHA (Hazen) Color Assessment in Liquids
content: A portable smartphone-based colorimetric sensing system was developed and experimentally evaluated for rapid APHA/Hazen color screening using controlled image acquisition and blank-corrected differential RGB responses. APHA platinum–cobalt standards in the range of 50–500 PCU were analyzed by UV–Vis spectrophotometry and by a smartphone coupled to a 3D-printed dark chamber. The reference UV–Vis measurements showed excellent linearity between APHA level and absorbance at 455 nm (R2 ≈ 0.9998), confirming the suitability of the spectrophotometric method as the analytical reference. In contrast, the smartphone-derived differential RGB responses exhibited concentration-dependent but non-monotonic behavior over the investigated APHA range, reflecting the influence of chromatic redistribution, optical geometry, surface reflections, and imaging conditions. These responses should therefore be interpreted as device-dependent broadband colorimetric descriptors rather than direct absorbance measurements. An exploratory first-order multivariate regression model based on ∆R, ∆G, and ∆B was evaluated to investigate the empirical relationship between the RGB descriptors and the reference absorbance at 455 nm. The full calibration fit yielded R2 = 0.9487, RMSE =0.0102, and MAE=0.0082absorbance units; however, leave-one-level-out validation showed reduced predictive robustness (R2 = 0.8445, RMSE = 0.0178, and MAE = 0.0152 absorbance units), and the residual structure indicated concentration-dependent lack of fit. Therefore, the multivariate model should not be regarded as a validated quantitative calibration for APHA determination, but rather as an exploratory empirical relationship showing that smartphone-derived RGB descriptors retain partial colorimetric information under controlled portable conditions. The proposed system is suitable as a low-cost, field-deployable tool for preliminary semiquantitative screening of transparent liquid samples. At the same time, laboratory UV–Vis spectrophotometry remains the preferred confirmatory method when higher analytical accuracy, traceability, or regulatory compliance is required.
